text.p: Slovakia's widely boycotted weekend referendum was declared officially void on Monday and a member of the Central Referendum Committee denounced ballot papers distributed by the Interior Ministry as a "massive swindle".
The committee refused even to count the result, saying the small number of voters who went to the polls on Friday and Saturday wasted their time because the ballots were illegal.

The referendum had been a test for democracy in Slovakia, which broke out of the Czechoslovak federation after the collapse of communism but has come under fire from the West and wanted to revive its fading hopes of an invitation to join NATO.

Instead, the vote was turned into chaos by Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's long-running rivalry with President Michal Kovac, who wanted a question about presidential elections on the ballot and led the boycott when it was struck off at the last moment.
Kovac and his supporters want future presidents elected directly, a change that might head off the ambitions of Meciar, who could inherit presidential powers if the choice remains with parliament.
Interior Minister Gustav Krajci removed the election question from the ballots at the last minute, claiming the Constitutional Court had declared it illegal.
The government tried to go ahead with the remaining ballot asking whether Slovaks want to join NATO. But many thousands of electors followed the president in refusing to take part.
"The referendum... was nullified," Referendum Committee vice-chairman Jozef Krumpolec told a news conference.

"The total number of eligible voters taking part in the vote was nil. The number of citizens who replied "Yes" and those who replied "No" cannot be assessed because no (valid) ballot papers were delivered."
Committee member Kalman Petocz told reporters the panel had lodged a complaint with state prosecutors over the interior minister's last minute change in the ballot.

"Unfortunately, the committee had no means to prevent this, the most massive swindle on citizens so far," he said. "Any alleged number (of votes) is completely false and cannot be considered even as an opinion poll."

"I call on Premier Meciar to resign for what he did with the referendum," Christian Democratic Movement leader Jan Carnogursky said on Monday. "This government has no longer the authority and international stature to be able to ensure the economic and political security of Slovakia."

Meciar acknowledged to a Sunday news conference less than 10 percent of Slovakia's 3.4 million electors voted, but blamed his opponents. "The chaos began when... political parties and the president wrote to the mayors telling them to ignore the government," Meciar said.
